title: The Truth with Stephen Mangan - Theatre Review
transcript: Hello and welcome to Theatre Reviews With Paul Seven. I'm here at the Apollo Theatre in Shaftesbury Avenue to see The Truth. What can I say about The Truth? No, I mean literally what am I allowed to say about this comedy by Florian Zeller? I can describe for you the first scene, but after that twist follows revelation, follows surprise, follows discovery, follows bewilderment. So much so that to say anything may be to say too much. What I can tell you is that the four actors in this are fabulously funny. Keep watching and I'll tell you a lot more. But first, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel. And also visit my website, theatre dot reviews, where you'll find my reviews of not only this play, but hundreds of others and my roundups of other critics reviews, including of The Truth. So, what is the truth about The Truth? Well, in the first scene, we find Michel, played by Steven Mangan, in bed with Alice, played by Sarah Hadland. They're having an affair. It turns out Alice's husband, Paul, is Michel's best friend. And her lover seems more guilty about betraying him than his wife. In fact, Michel seems to think it quite normal to commit adultery. And for her part, well, she'd like a little more than a quick weekly get together, but doesn't seem to want to actually leave her husband any more than he wants to leave his wife. Six more scenes follow in which Michel meets each of the other three twice, all two person scenes. The second scene sets the pattern for the rest of the play. And if this play has a fault, it is that it does get a bit repetitive. So Michel is with his wife Laurence, played by Janie Dee, who seems suspicious about what he might be up to. He gets more and more tied up in his casual lies and stutters his way into further deceits. Somewhere along the the way truth sometimes seems like a lie and sometimes well is a lie and what seems like a lie can turn out to be true. Even after an hour and a half without interval, questions of what is true and what is a deception are still left hanging deliciously for us to chew on as we leave. Florian Zeller's companion piece, The Lie, that followed The Truth a few years later and featured what appeared to be the same characters explores the notion in more depth that deception makes the world go round and truth brings it to a halt. But it is a more serious play. The Truth is an out-out comedy written before Zeller got into reverse theatre in a big way, the kind that causes us to question truth and reality by showing us scenes from various subjective perspectives. Something that reached the height of confusion in his latest play on the subject of adultery, The Forest. Here, all the fun is in what the characters say and don't say and how they react to what they're told. And in an extension of that, how we as an audience react, knowing what we think we know and then finding out we didn't know after all. The casting is perfect. The play stands or falls on the strength of the actor playing Michel, and in Steven Mangan they have made the perfect choice. But I think the problem is that really this play is about Michelle making a fool of himself and it's not even clear at the end that he's learned anything from it. Steven Mangan is like a naughty child crashing into his own constructions like a toddler learning to walk, shouting as a way of defending himself and even at one point sitting sulkily in the corner with a big bottom lip. He not only doesn't listen to others, he doesn't seem to hear himself being so self-centred that he cannot see the hypocrisy of being outraged by the betrayal of his friend deliberately losing at tennis. but oblivious to the upset caused by the revelation of his betrayal of his wife and friend. Janie Dee's facial expressions are quite brilliant. A slight widening of her eyes becomes as revelatory as a whole speech. Ardal O'Hanlan as Paul quietly hides behind a neat beard, displaying a tight smile and a penetrating look that could be concealing either a secret or some feeling. Even Sarah Hadland's emotive Alice appears to have something up the sleeve she seems to wear her heart on. You're watching Theatre Reviews with Paul Seven. I've reviewed hundreds of shows over the last eight years, so please explore my back catalogue. You might also like to visit my website, theater dot reviews where you'll find written versions of all my reviews and also my roundups of other critics reviews. And by the way, The truth received a range of ratings from five stars to two. In Lizzie Clachan's set design, hotels, a changing room, and sitting rooms all look similarly anodyne. And there's even a joke about hotel rooms looking the same. It all suggests an emptiness to these characters' lives. There's a familiarity about the creative team. This is a translation by Christopher Hampton, who has brought seven of Zeller's plays to English-speaking audiences, including most famously The Father. Director Lindsay Posner has previously directed The Truth and The Lie at the Menier. And we should probably be thankful that he moves the production with such a pace that we've no time to dwell on some of the more unlikely or more repetitive elements of the plot. The Truth is a straightforward comedy and pretty funny compared with Zeller's other hits. You can argue that there are some profound points about the importance of deception to human society and it may also have become more relevant in an age of in which media and leaders give equal weight to truth and lies. I think I've said enough. I give The Truth three stars. I hope you found this review useful and interesting. If you did, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel. Then you'll be the first to know about my future reviews. And you can read this review on my website, theater dot reviews, along with my roundup of other critics' reviews of The Truth. And you have the opportunity to add your own review and rating if you've seen this show. And you can follow me on the usual social media. Thank you for watching.
